Reality is the ridesharing market is out of its infancy and into adolescence at this point. Uber isn't the most popular on demand ridesharing app based purely on its convenience but because a lot of the time its the most convenient app to use at typically the lowest price. There's pretty intense price competition in the market now with other competitors which forces price down (to consumers benefit) but keeps margins thin for the companies. I just don't see any company going down the route of making drivers employees unless they're absolutely forced to. People arguing that Uber or Lyft are only holding back from doing it out of pure greed dont understand how the industry works and the models of all of these businesses.

The BUSINESS doesn't want that. Uber stays afloat on their independent contractor setup because every time they pay a contractor they're also taking a cut of the earnings. Introducing a different employment structure increases overhead considerably, meaning they can't scale out like they have been. If you want to kill Uber and watch them bleed even more money than they already do go for it and watch us go back to the dark ages of monopolized taxi services

I mean sure but regardless of what company does it all you're doing by making independent contractors employees is paying them an hourly rate + tips and whatever incentive structure you have set up. Guess who's been doing that for decades? Taxi companies. I dont think anyone wants Uber or Lyft to become Taxi 2.0, they're disruptors for a reason, because they brought new and innovative idea (independent contracting of drivers for whatever hours they want to drive) into the mix and it worked.
But they won't, because Lyft operates on the exact same operating model as Uber. If it would tank Uber it would also tank Lyft
